# Cardiovascular disease & hypertension

> *The insulin resistance and abnormal blood lipids that run through obesity and type 2 diabetes also
> show up as raised blood pressure and atherosclerosis. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of
> death in Singapore, and much of its risk is modifiable by diet: the salt in hawker soups and sauces,
> and the kind of fat in the cooking oil.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how saturated and *trans* fat, by raising LDL cholesterol, build atherosclerotic plaque, and how
  sodium raises blood pressure.
- Describe how far the DASH pattern lowers blood pressure, how it adds to sodium reduction, and the
  limits of its evidence.
- Explain why the benefit of cutting saturated fat depends on what replaces it.
- Distinguish oily fish, routine omega-3 supplements and prescription icosapent ethyl by their evidence.
- Explain why alcohol is never advised for heart protection, although cutting down lowers blood pressure.
- Check for kidney disease and potassium-raising medicines before advising a potassium salt substitute,
  and refer for risk-tiered blood-pressure and cholesterol targets.
:::

## Cardiovascular disease & hypertension at a glance {#sec-overview}

Two facts set the stakes. Cardiovascular disease causes about 30% of all deaths in Singapore, and
roughly one in three adults has **hypertension** (persistently raised blood pressure), just over half of them
undiagnosed [@shfHeartStats2024; @nphs2024]. The response is population-scale **primary prevention**
(preventing disease before it develops), delivered lifestyle-first.

Three principles frame the advice and the referral:

- The modern framing treats heart-healthy eating as a whole dietary pattern, not a list of good and bad
  nutrients [@aha2021diet].
- At this stage the task is to recognise the dietary changes that lower risk and refer or co-manage
  for the plan: a dietitian delivers the structured change, and drug decisions belong to the clinician.
- Blood-pressure and cholesterol targets are risk-tiered and looked up, not memorised; it is enough to
  know that they exist and are individualised.

The American Heart Association organises heart-healthy eating around these features [@aha2021diet]:

- plenty of fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and legumes;
- fish and plant proteins;
- liquid plant oils over tropical or hydrogenated fats;
- minimally processed over ultra-processed foods;
- little added sugar or salt.

The WHO adds population targets: salt under 5 g a day, saturated fat under 10% of energy, *trans* fat under
1%, free sugars under 10%, and at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day [@who2020diet]. DASH, sodium
reduction, fat quality and the Mediterranean pattern all sit within this pattern, and Singapore's My
Healthy Plate is its local form, which needs no counting of nutrients [@hpbHealthyPlate].

## Pathophysiology: how diet affects the arteries and blood pressure {#sec-cvd-science}

Diet raises blood pressure and promotes atherosclerosis mainly through two pathways, and both converge
on the vessel wall. Both pathways build on how fats are carried as lipoproteins (see the
[*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) and
[*Integrative Metabolism*](integrative-metabolism.qmd#sec-lipoproteins) chapters) and how sodium
and water balance is regulated (see the
[*Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter). Four terms recur
below:

Atherosclerosis
: The build-up of plaque in the artery wall, where LDL cholesterol is deposited and inflames the wall;
  the plaque narrows the vessel and can rupture.

Vascular tone
: How constricted the blood vessels are; higher tone raises blood pressure.

Endothelium
: The inner lining of a blood vessel.

Dyslipidaemia
: An abnormal pattern of blood lipids, the cholesterol and triglycerides carried in lipoproteins.

![Two dietary pathways converge on the artery: saturated and trans fat raise LDL cholesterol, which builds atherosclerotic plaque in the artery wall; dietary sodium raises blood volume and vascular tone, raising blood pressure (dietary potassium counter-regulates). Both damage the vessel and drive heart attack and stroke.](/figures/mechanisms/cvd-diet-pathways.svg){#fig-cvd-pathways width="90%" fig-align="center"}

**Dietary fat and LDL.** Dietary saturated and *trans* fat raise LDL cholesterol, the "bad" cholesterol
carried in low-density lipoproteins [@mensink2003]. LDL is deposited in the artery wall and inflames it,
building the atherosclerotic plaque that narrows vessels and, when it ruptures, causes heart attacks and
strokes. Improving fat quality ([below](#sec-cvd-fat)) therefore measurably cuts cardiovascular events
[@hooper2020; @sacks2017].

**Sodium, potassium and blood pressure.** Dietary sodium expands blood volume and raises vascular tone,
pushing blood pressure up in a graded, dose-dependent way [@he2013saltbp; @huang2020sodiumdose]. Dietary
potassium works the other way, helping the kidney excrete sodium and relaxing the vessels
[@who2012potassium].

Blood pressure and plaque then act on the same endothelium, and the insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia
of obesity and type 2 diabetes feed both pathways (see the *Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome* and *Type 2
Diabetes* chapters).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: salt and saturated fat act on different things. Why can cutting either one lower the risk of heart attack and stroke?
Saturated and *trans* fat raise LDL cholesterol, which is deposited in the artery wall and builds
atherosclerotic plaque; sodium raises blood pressure by expanding blood volume and raising vascular
tone. The pressure and the plaque act on the same endothelium, and plaque that narrows a vessel can
rupture, causing heart attacks and strokes. Easing either pathway therefore reduces the damage to the
vessel wall.
:::

## Lowering blood pressure {#sec-cvd-pressure}

### The DASH dietary pattern {#sec-cvd-dash}

The DASH pattern (rich in fruit, vegetables, wholegrains and low-fat dairy; see the
[*What a Healthy Diet Looks Like*](dietary-guidelines-patterns.qmd) chapter) was designed to lower blood
pressure, and it does so in its own right. In the landmark feeding trial, with sodium and weight held
constant, it lowered blood pressure by about 5.5/3.0 mmHg overall and 11.4/5.5 mmHg in people with
hypertension, so the effect came from the pattern itself [@appel1997dash]. Two caveats apply. The trial
was a short controlled-feeding study with a surrogate endpoint (blood pressure), and people following the
pattern on their own achieve less, with pooled trials nearer 3–7/2–4 mmHg [@filippou2020dashmeta;
@appel2003premier]. Even so, a few mmHg across a population meaningfully lowers stroke and heart disease.

DASH works through the whole-food matrix (potassium, magnesium and fibre together), which beats the
matched supplements, so the advice is *potassium-rich produce, not pills* [@alsolaiman2010dashmechanism].
DASH also adds to salt reduction: in DASH-Sodium, each change lowered blood pressure on its own, and the
two together lowered it most [@sacks2001dashsodium]. In Singapore, My Healthy Plate carries the core of
DASH into everyday meals: half the plate fruit and vegetables, a quarter wholegrains, a quarter lean
protein [@hpbHealthyPlate].

### Sodium reduction and potassium intake {#sec-cvd-sodium}

Sodium is Singapore's headline dietary problem (see the *Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes*
chapter). About 9 in 10 residents exceed the recommended sodium limit, averaging about 3,600 mg a day
(roughly twice the WHO ceiling), and most of it is hidden in soup bases, sauces, seasonings and food eaten
out, not added from the salt shaker [@hpb2023sodium]. The blood-pressure benefit of cutting back is
graded and reversible [@he2013saltbp], and the complementary change is eating more potassium (fruit,
vegetables, legumes).

The **sodium J-curve**, the suggestion that very low salt intake is harmful, is largely a measurement
artefact, and it is irrelevant at Singapore's high average intake, where essentially everyone benefits
from cutting down [@cappuccio2022sodiummyths].

One option with hard-outcome support is a potassium-enriched salt substitute, which in a large trial cut
strokes and deaths [@neal2021ssass]. It is not safe for everyone.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check the kidneys before a potassium salt substitute
Potassium-based salt substitutes are helpful for *most* people, but the trial that proved they work
**excluded people with serious kidney disease and those taking potassium-sparing diuretics or
potassium supplements** [@neal2021ssass]. Two other common blood-pressure drugs also raise blood
potassium: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). In
all of these people, extra potassium can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia, a high blood potassium that can disturb heart
rhythm. So before recommending one, check for kidney disease and those medications, and if in doubt,
don't. (For the renal side of potassium, see the *Chronic Kidney Disease* chapter.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
The salt is in the soup, the gravy and the sauces, not mainly the shaker: a bowl of fishball noodle
*soup* can carry most of a day's sodium. The practical swaps to advise are made at the stall:

- Leave most of the soup.
- Ask for "less salt".
- Take sauce or gravy on the side.
- Skip the extra soy and chilli.
- Choose steamed over deep-fried.
- Add vegetables and fruit for potassium.

Nationally, look for the "Lower in Sodium" Healthier Choice Symbol; Nutri-Grade is also being extended
beyond drinks to sauces, seasonings and instant noodles [@hpb2023sodium; @moh2025nutrigrade].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: the DASH trial held sodium and weight constant. What follows for a patient who is already cutting salt?
Because sodium and weight did not change, the fall in blood pressure came from the pattern itself,
through its whole-food mix of potassium, magnesium and fibre. In DASH-Sodium each change lowered blood
pressure on its own and the two together lowered it most, so the patient gains more by adding the
pattern (in Singapore, My Healthy Plate) to the salt reduction.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a hawker-centre regular never adds salt at the table. Why can his sodium intake still be about twice the WHO ceiling?
Most sodium in Singapore is already in the soup bases, sauces, seasonings and food eaten out before the
food reaches the table, so leaving out the salt shaker removes little of it. A bowl of fishball noodle
soup can carry most of a day's sodium on its own. The swaps that help are made at the stall: leaving
most of the soup, taking sauce on the side and asking for less salt.
:::

## Protecting the arteries {#sec-cvd-artery}

### Dietary fat: quality and replacement {#sec-cvd-fat}

What matters for the heart is the quality of dietary fat and what replaces it, rather than the total
amount (see the *Macronutrients* chapter). Swapping saturated and *trans* fat for unsaturated fat lowers
LDL cholesterol and cuts cardiovascular events: reducing saturated fat cuts events by around 17%, and
replacing it specifically with polyunsaturated fat cuts them by roughly 30%, about the effect of a
**statin**, a cholesterol-lowering drug [@mensink2003; @hooper2020; @sacks2017].

The widely reported "saturated fat has been exonerated" headlines came from studies that did not say what
the fat was replaced with [@siritarino2010], and when the replacement is refined carbohydrate and sugar,
there is no benefit [@sacks2017]. The question to ask of every swap is therefore "replaced with what?": butter or palm oil
for olive or canola oil, yes; butter for white bread, no. Try each replacement below.

<div data-island="fat-swap" data-src="/diagrams/fat-swap.yml"></div>

### Oily fish, omega-3 supplements and icosapent ethyl {#sec-cvd-fish}

A common patient question is whether to buy fish-oil capsules "for the heart". The answer separates three
different things:

- Oily fish is a food to recommend, as part of the pattern.
- Routine omega-3 supplements failed to prevent cardiovascular events in large trials
  [@manson2019vital; @ascend2018omega3], so the advice is the fish, not the capsule.
- Prescription **icosapent ethyl**, tested in the "fish-oil trial" people cite, is a high-dose drug used in
  selected patients [@bhatt2019reduceit]; prescribing it is a specialist decision, and its result does not
  extend to over-the-counter fish oil.

![Oily fish such as salmon is a food to recommend for heart health, though that is not the same as an over-the-counter fish-oil capsule.](/figures/food/grilled-salmon.jpg){#fig-oily-fish width="55%" fig-align="center"}

### The Mediterranean dietary pattern {#sec-cvd-mediterranean}

The Mediterranean pattern (olive oil, nuts, fish, vegetables, legumes, wholegrains; see the *What a
Healthy Diet Looks Like* chapter) is the one with event-level trial evidence. In PREDIMED it lowered a
composite of cardiovascular events by about 30% in relative terms in a high-risk Spanish population, a
signal driven mainly by stroke [@estruch2018predimed].

The evidence carries two caveats. First, the effect is a relative reduction on a composite endpoint in a
high-risk group, so it does not promise a 30% cut for everyone. Second, the original 2013 paper was
retracted and republished in 2018 after randomisation irregularities, with its conclusion upheld: science
self-correcting, not a diet debunked.

Guidelines endorse the pattern itself rather than a specific percentage reduction [@esc2021prevention;
@medUmbrella]. The everyday translation is, again, My Healthy Plate: plants, wholegrains, fish and plant
oils.

### Alcohol and cardiovascular risk {#sec-cvd-alcohol}

The old reassurance that "a daily glass protects your heart" has not held up. The apparent benefit came
from comparing drinkers with an "abstainer" group that included people who had stopped drinking because
they were ill (see the [*Adulthood & Working Life*](adulthood-working-life.qmd) chapter); Mendelian
randomisation studies, which use genetic variants to remove that bias, find risk rising with intake and
no protective threshold [@biddinger2022mralcohol], and health bodies now state that there is no safe
level [@who2023nosafelevel].

Cutting down does lower blood pressure, dose-dependently and most in heavy drinkers
[@roerecke2017bp], and because heavy drinking raises triglycerides, cutting down or stopping is the
standard advice when they are high [@klop2013alcoholtg]. Alcohol reduction is therefore a cardiovascular measure for people who
drink, but never a reason for anyone to start. Singapore's low-risk guidance caps intake at about two
standard drinks a day for men and one for women (a standard drink is about 10 g of alcohol), a
harm-reduction ceiling, not a "safe" target [@mohAlcoholLimits2018].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient gives up butter and eats more white bread instead. Why is his cardiovascular risk unlikely to fall?
The benefit of cutting saturated fat depends on what replaces it. Replacing it with unsaturated fat
lowers LDL cholesterol and cuts events, by roughly 30% when the replacement is polyunsaturated fat, but
replacing it with refined carbohydrate and sugar brings no benefit. Butter for olive or canola oil is
the swap that helps; butter for white bread is not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: one patient wants omega-3 capsules because of the "fish-oil trial"; a non-drinker asks whether daily wine protects the heart. Why does the evidence support neither?
The "fish-oil trial" tested icosapent ethyl, a high-dose prescription drug, so its result does not extend
to over-the-counter fish oil, and prescribing it is a specialist decision. Routine omega-3 supplements
failed to prevent cardiovascular events in large trials, so the advice is to eat oily fish as part of
the pattern.

The apparent protection from alcohol came from comparing drinkers with "abstainer" groups that included
people who had stopped drinking because they were ill, and genetic studies that remove this bias find
risk rising with intake and no protective threshold. Cutting down lowers blood pressure in people who
already drink, but that is never a reason to start, so advise the non-drinker not to.
:::

## What does a heart-healthy plate look like? {#sec-close}

The evidence points to a pattern of eating:

- Plenty of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and legumes.
- Fish and plant proteins.
- Unsaturated oils in place of saturated and *trans* fat ("replaced with what?").
- Salt down and potassium up.
- Oily fish, not fish-oil capsules.
- No alcohol taken up for the heart.

In Singapore that is My Healthy Plate at the hawker stall: less soup and gravy, brown rice, more
vegetables and a *teh-o kosong*.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**The burden is large, and much of it is silent.** Cardiovascular disease is Singapore's leading cause of
death, about 30% of deaths [@shfHeartStats2024]. Measured hypertension, a silent driver of that burden,
affects about 34% of adults, but just over half of them are undiagnosed and most known cases are not well
controlled [@nphs2024]. The gap between self-reported and measured hypertension is the case for screening
a disease that has no symptoms.

**The dietary changes have national counterparts.** Sodium is the priority ([above](#sec-cvd-sodium)),
and national measures target it: a target to cut intake by 15% by 2026, subsidies for reduced-sodium
ingredients, and the Nutri-Grade extension to sauces and instant noodles [@hpb2023sodium;
@moh2025nutrigrade]. For fats, cooking oil is the single largest local source of saturated fat, so the
change to make at home is the type of oil and less deep-frying [@moh2025nutrigrade]. My Healthy Plate is
the ready-made local form of the DASH and Mediterranean patterns [@hpbHealthyPlate].

**Risk is estimated, and the tool must fit the population.** Singapore estimates risk with SG-FRS-2023, a
risk score recalibrated on local multi-ethnic data because imported US equations mis-estimate risk across
Chinese, Malay and Indian groups; it estimates only 10-year coronary risk, not stroke or total
cardiovascular risk [@sgfrs2023]. The national clinical guidances on hypertension and lipids, from the
Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE), are risk-tiered and lifestyle-first [@aceHtn2023; @aceLipid2023].
Structured dietary change is referred through EatWise SG [@mohEatWiseSG] (see the *Interprofessional
Practice & Referral* chapter).

::: {.callout-important}
## Blood-pressure and cholesterol targets: risk-tiered and looked up
No single cholesterol or blood-pressure target applies to every patient. Targets are **risk-tiered**: a
clinician estimates cardiovascular risk (in Singapore, with SG-FRS-2023), and the ACE guidance gives the
individual's target. At this stage, recognise that targets exist, are individualised and are looked up.
Then deliver the lifestyle advice and refer, instead of applying drug thresholds from memory
[@aceHtn2023; @aceLipid2023].
:::

## Practise: Mr Chua, hawker meals, blood pressure and cholesterol {#sec-case}

Mr Chua is 52, eats most meals at the hawker centre, and has a raised blood pressure and LDL cholesterol.
He wants to know whether he needs medication, whether to buy a potassium salt substitute he saw online,
and whether a daily beer is good for his heart. Work through the visit: lead with the right first move,
translate the pattern to his hawker plate, handle the salt-substitute safety check, and notice where
memorising a target, or reaching for a drug first, would be the wrong reflex. Your choices branch the
case.
